extracted.intended_audience: economists, policymakers, graduate students and analysts interested in macroeconomic policy and international monetary integration
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for evaluating national macroeconomic policy credibility (monetary and fiscal discipline), suitability for participation in a monetary union, and exposure to international market sanctions. Focuses on how markets, institutions and policy choices affect interest rates, exchange rates, and risk premia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary discipline / price stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Central banks should pursue price stability; the document repeatedly highlights the Bundesbank and the objective of stability of prices as the cornerstone of credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit, sustained commitment to price stability raises a country's credibility on international financial markets, lowers real interest rates and reduces the risk premium. The text notes that countries that commit to price stability (e.g., Germany, Japan) enjoy more favorable conditions on international markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgetary discipline / fiscal balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments must restrain budget deficits and reduce public dissaving; large and persistent fiscal deficits increase the debt burden and raise interest costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High deficits lead to accumulation of external debt, higher interest payments (example: Canada's external debt and interest burden), and elevated risk premia. Reducing the fiscal deficit is necessary to regain market confidence and to lower sovereign borrowing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central bank independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A central bank must be autonomous from government to anchor monetary credibility (e.g., Bundesbank example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence allows commitment to anti-inflationary policy; proposed features include an independent European central bank with no government holdings. Independence helps countries 'import' credibility (via membership) and reduces market-imposed risk premia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of deficit monetization and no-bailout rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary financing (monétisation) of government deficits must be avoided; the union should exclude the possibility of member bailouts (renflouement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent moral hazard and preserve discipline, institutional rules should bar central bank purchases of national debt and forbid mutualized bailouts. This reduces incentives for irresponsible fiscal expansion within a monetary union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance and enforcement within a monetary union
rubrics_metrics.description: A monetary union requires surveillance mechanisms, parliamentary/institutional oversight and the power to recommend corrective measures to members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective peer surveillance (as in the European Community example) and formal institutions enable peer pressure to enforce discipline; absence of such institutions (as with G7) leads to weak coordination and ad hoc outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry criteria for monetary union (fiscal ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish fiscal/ debt-to-GDP ratio criteria for admission to a monetary union to avoid fragile entrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry requirements (ratios of debt to national output) are proposed to prevent countries with already-high debt from joining and creating systemic risks. The text suggests using such numerical thresholds as part of institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market discipline and risk premia
rubrics_metrics.description: International financial markets will impose risk premiums on countries perceived as fiscally or monetarily indisciplined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markets react via higher short- and long-term interest rates and exchange-rate pressures; these premiums serve as sanctions and increase the cost of borrowing, potentially forcing corrective policy action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital mobility and external constraints on policy
rubrics_metrics.description: With high capital mobility, international markets largely determine interest rates and constrain domestic stabilization policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The integration of financial markets means governments have less room to use independent monetary or fiscal stimulus without incurring exchange-rate depreciation or higher risk premia; policy choices must account for international capital flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding inflationary monetary policy
rubrics_metrics.description: An inflationary monetary expansion intended to stimulate activity can reduce private saving and invite market sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inflationary monetary policies may temporarily lower interest rates and stimulate activity, but their delayed costs (inflation, lower private saving) lead to higher risk premia and exchange-rate penalties, as in the UK experience described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal policy restraint when monetary instrument lost
rubrics_metrics.description: If membership in a monetary union removes national monetary instruments, fiscal policy must be used parsimoniously and be constrained to prevent excessive deficits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without national monetary control, unchecked fiscal expansion will raise community-wide interest rates; institutional constraints and peer surveillance are needed to prevent spillovers and preserve union stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of private and public saving rates
rubrics_metrics.description: National availability of savings (private and public) determines ability to finance investment; declining national saving raises real interest rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document emphasizes that falling private saving (aging, social security, credit deregulation) and rising public dissaving are key causes of reduced national saving; reversing public dissaving can notably improve national saving rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public dissaving's crowding out of productive investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public dissaving (government borrowing to finance current spending) can crowd out private investment and reduce future productivity and competitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If government borrowing finances consumption rather than productive investment, the capital stock available to labor is lower, damaging long-run competitiveness and export performance (example applied to Canada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitiveness, productivity growth and policy mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained productivity gains and investment-oriented saving are necessary for external surpluses and long-term market standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High private saving channeled into productive investment (Japan example) supported export-led competitiveness and current-account surpluses; policy should favor investment-enhancing uses of saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of institutional integration and peer pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic/historic integration and institutional structures (parliament, surveillance bodies) strengthen the effectiveness of peer pressure for policy discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CE (EU) example shows that shared institutions, large intra-area trade, and formal oversight create credible peer pressure that enforces commitments and discourages deviant policy conduct more effectively than loose groups like the G7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and incentives of indiscipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments have incentives to be temporarily indisciplined (immediate gains) while costs are delayed and partly borne by private agents or trade partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because benefits of expansion are immediate and costs postponed, without external constraints or institutions countries will tend to 'cheat'; this justifies coordination or binding rules to internalize cross-border costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numerical/empirical indicators (interest rates, current account, debt ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate countries using observable indicators: short- and long-term interest rates, current account balances, private saving rates, government budget balances, and debt-to-GDP ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report relies on tables showing real interest rates, current account, private saving, and budget balances across countries and decades; these indicators reveal market assessments and the impact of policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overreliance on external financing
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive dependence on foreign saving to finance consumption or deficits increases vulnerability to shifts in international investor sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries that finance consumption (versus investment) with foreign funds (example: Canada in the 1980s) face larger external debt burdens and fiercer market disciplining when international conditions change.
